extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society, natural philosophers, instrument-makers, and practitioners in agriculture and husbandry (17th-century scientists and skilled artisans)
extracted.subtask_description: A questionnaire / set of enquiries designed to collect faithful, practical information about agriculture and husbandry across regions (arable and meadow practices, soils, crops, instruments, yields, pests, preservation, etc.). Intended to be distributed to experienced persons for compiling a history and improvements of agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for piercing rock and blasting with double wedge and gunpowder
rubrics_metrics.description: Tool of iron, well steeled at the end (20 or 21 inches long, ~2 1/2 inches diameter at steeled end), steeled end shaped to pierce rock with more obtuse angles for harder rock; hold tool by hand where hole to be made (near bottom), strike with heavy hammer (one man hammers while another holds tool); after each stroke turn the point a little so fresh edges strike; continue until hole 18–20 inches deep (deeper the better). Fit a kind of double wedge exactly into the hole (each piece 12–13 inches long, forming a diagonal-cut cylinder); grease contiguous flat sides; in upper wedge cut a hollow crease/groove round about to fasten a cartridge full of gunpowder (about half a pound or more); wedge must have a priming hole drilled through length to be filled with priming powder; place cartridge and wedges home so they both fit exactly; lay priming powder on the flattened end of lower wedge and fasten a slow-burning match/thread (dipped in brimstone or similar) so workman may retire; place a piece of wood or iron as a brace against the lower wedge so it cannot slip. When powder fires it drives out the upper wedge and, by its slant, wedges thicker as it retreats until stopped; the inflamed powder then tears and cracks the rock, often blowing out or breaking a large quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes dimensions and materials; stresses exact fitting of wedges, lubrication of contacting faces, priming through a drilled hole, slow-burning fuse to allow retreat, and safety brace to prevent slip. Emphasizes deeper holes (18–20 in or deeper) for effectiveness and use of heavy hammering with rotation between blows to remove chips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions for Planting White Mulberries (silkworks foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, he teaches the means of sowing, planting, and raising white mulberries (as the foundation of silkworks) showing how many several ways that may be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author regards the white mulberry-tree as preferable to the black for durableness of wood, fitness of leaves for feeding silkworms and livestock, and for berries to fatten poultry; practical methods and multiple ways of sowing/raising should be described in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breeding silkworms: eggs, hatching, feeding, disease prevention and cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, The breeding of silkworms, the choosing of good eggs, and their hatching, as also the feeding of the worms, and preserving them from sickness, and curing them of it, together with the way of making them spin to best advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance includes choosing good eggs, methods of hatching, feeding regimens, ventilation (open windows when weather permits), avoiding interruptions during spinning, and remedies/preservation techniques to keep worms healthy and spinning properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of winding silk and instruments needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, The manner of winding their silk from their bottoms, adding the scheme of the instrument serving for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The winding process is called the most painful and nicest part; book gives very particular instructions concerning the way of winding off the silk, and sets down the form of the oven and instruments necessary for that work; emphasizes speed in winding off silk once cases are finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping silkworm eggs for the ensuing year
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourthly, The way of keeping silkworms' eggs for the ensuing year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes practical methods for preserving eggs across seasons; selection of cases and storage conditions are important for seed viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for white mulberry and uses of its leaves/fruit
rubrics_metrics.description: The white mulberry-tree, as it is in other qualities preferable to the black, so this author esteems it the best, not only for the durableness of the wood, and its large extent of usefulness in carpenters' and joiners' work; but also for the fitness of its leaves (besides their principal use for the food of silkworms) to fatten sheep, goats, cows, and hogs, only by boiling and mingling them with bran. The berries themselves he commends as very excellent to fatten poultry, and to make them lay eggs plentifully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to prefer white mulberry for multiple agricultural and husbandry benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventilation and handling of silkworms during late feeding/spinning
rubrics_metrics.description: Silkworms, before they begin to spin, and about the latter end of their feeding, must, says the author, be often changed, and have air enough, by opening the windows of the room they are in, if it be not too severe weather; else the silk in their belly will cause extraordinary heat, burn their guts, sometimes burst them, and the substance will putrefy into a yellowish matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain adequate ventilation (open windows when safe); avoid overheating or crowding that causes internal issues and spoilage of silk; change ( presumably their bedding/position) often near spinning time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never interrupt silkworms while spinning
rubrics_metrics.description: He advertises, that they must by no means be interrupted in their work, to the end, that all the silk they have in their bellies may come out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disturb worms during the spinning process to ensure full extraction of silk from the caterpillar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and selection of cases for seed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some eight days after they have finished their work, as many of the best cases as are to serve for seed, viz. the first done, the hardest, the reddest and best coloured, must be chosen, and put apart; and all diligence is to be used to wind off the silk with as much speed as may be, especially if the worms have nimbly dispatched their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the earliest/ hardest/ reddest/ best-coloured cases as seed; wind off silk promptly, prioritizing speed when worms finish quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and sequence of silkworm spinning (3-day process)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first day they make only a web; the second, they form in this web their cases, and cover themselves all over with silk; the third day, they are no longer seen; and the days following they thicken their cases, always by one end or thread, which they never break off themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the normal timeline of silk-case construction informs collection and intervention timing; note continuous single-thread spinning behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for breeding cases and mating procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Touching their generation, he prescribes that there be chosen as many male as female cases (which are discerned by this, that the males are more pointed at both ends of the cases, and the females more obtuse on the ends, and bigger-bellied), and that care be had, that no cases be taken, but such wherein the worms are heard rolling; which done, and they being come forth in the form of butterflies, having four wings, six feet, two horns, and two very black eyes, and put in a convenient place, the males fluttering with their wings, will join and couple with the females, after that these have first purged themselves of a kind of reddish humour: they are to be left from morning (which is the ordinary time of their coming forth) till evening, and then the females are to be gently pulled away, whereupon they will lay their eggs; but the males are then thrown away as useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed morphological criteria for sexing (case shape) and behavioural protocol for mating and egg-laying; discard males after mating for breeding stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 1 (kinds of soils and preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The several kinds of soils in England, being supposed to be either sandy, gravelly, stony, clayey, chalky, light-mould, heathy, marsh, boggy, fenny, or cold weeping ground: what is the soil of each country, and how prepared for arable ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect regional soil-type inventories and standard preparation methods for turning each into arable ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 2 (soil preparation and manures for each grain)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. What peculiar preparation each soil undergoes for each kind of grain; with what kind of manure they are prepared; when, how, and in what quantity it is laid on ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record per-soil per-grain preparation protocols, manuring types, timings and quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 3 (ploughing seasons and plough types)
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. At what seasons and how often they are ploughed; and what kind of ploughs are used for several sorts of ground ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document ploughing frequency, seasonal schedules, and plough designs appropriate to soil types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 4 (fallow durations)
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. How long the several grounds are let lie fallow?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather typical fallow-period practices across regions and rotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 5 (improving heathy grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. How, and for what productions, heathy grounds may be improved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect methods for converting or improving heathland and the intended crops/productivity outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 6 (marl occurrence and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. What ground has marl ? how deep commonly it lies from the surface ? what is the depth of the marl itself? what the colour of it? upon what grounds it is used? what time of the year it is to be laid on? how many loads to an acre? what grains marled land will bear; and how many years together? how such marled land is to be used afterwards, &c. ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed field survey questions about marl deposits and practical guidelines for its application and effects on cropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 7 (kinds of grain and preparation for sowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. The kinds of grain or seed, usual in England, being either wheat, miscellane, rye, barley, oats, peas, beans, fitches, buck-wheat, hemp, flax, rape ; what sorts of these are sown in each county, and how prepared for sowing? whether by steeping, and in what kind of liquor ; or by mixing it, and with what ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record local varietal use and pre-sowing treatments (steeping, mixtures, media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 8 (which varietals grow where and their tillage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. There being many sorts of wheat, as the white or red lammas, the bearded Kentish wheat, the gray wheat, the red or gray pollard, the ducks-bill wheat, the red-eared bearded wheat, &c. And so of oats, as the common black, blue, naked, bearded in North-Wales, and the like of barley, peas, beans, &c. The inquiry is, which of these grow in each country, and in what soil ; which of them thrive best there, and whether each of them require a peculiar tillage, and how they differ in goodness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map varietal distribution, soil affinities, tillage requirements, and quality comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 9 (chief particulars in choice of seed-corn and succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. What are the chief particulars observable in the choice of seed-corn, and all kinds of grain ; and what kinds of grain are most proper to succeed each other ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture recommended seed-selection criteria and rotation/succession pairings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 10 (quantity sown and lunar/annual timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. What quantity of each kind is sown on the statute acre ? And in what season of the moon and year ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record seeding rates per statute acre and any timing rules tied to lunar or seasonal calendars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 11 (harrowing/clod-rolling instruments and seasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: 11. With what instruments they harrow, clod and rowl, and at what seasons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document implement types for surface preparation and their seasonal application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 12 (expected yields by quality of year)
rubrics_metrics.description: 12. How much an acre of good corn generally yields in very good, in less good, and in the worst years ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather statistical/typical yield ranges across variable years for planning and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 13 (causes and remedies of mildew, blasting, smut)
rubrics_metrics.description: 13. What are the causes and remedies of mildew, blasting, and smut; being some of the common diseases of corn in this country ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect causal theories and remedy practices for major cereal diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 14 (prevention of weeds, pests, birds, and animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: 14. How weeds, worms, flies, birds, mice, moles, &c. are prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document pest prevention and control methods for a range of nuisances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 15 (cutting/feeding young corn in the blade occasions and benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: 15. Upon what occasions young corn is cut or fed in the blade; and what are the benefits thereof ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record practices of cutting/feeding young corn, rationale, and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 16 (seasons and methods of reaping and ordering each sort before carting)
rubrics_metrics.description: 16. What are the seasons and ways of reaping and ordering each sort of grain, before it be carried off the ground ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect local harvest timing and handling/processing methods pre-storage or transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 17 (ways of preserving grain in straw from annoyances)
rubrics_metrics.description: 17. What are the several ways of preserving grain in the straw, within and without doors, from all annoyance, as mice, heating, rain, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record storage-in-field and barn techniques to protect unthreshed grain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 18 (ways of separating grain from straw and dressing them)
rubrics_metrics.description: 18. What are the several ways of separating the different sorts of grain from the straw, and of dressing them ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document threshing, winnowing, cleaning, and grading practices for different grains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Arable Grounds — 19 (ways of preserving any stores of grain from annoyances)
rubrics_metrics.description: 19. What are the ways of preserving any stores of grain from the annoyances they are liable to ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect storage, fumigation, drying, and other preservation measures for long-term grain stores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 1 (preparation of soils for pasture/meadow)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. How the above-mentioned sorts of soil are prepared, when they are used for pasture or meadow ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather preparation methods specific to pasture/meadow use adapted to each soil type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 2 (preventing common annoyances of pasture/meadow grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. How are prevented the common annoyances of these pasture or meadow grounds, as weeds, moss, sourgrass, heath, fern, bushes, briars, brambles, broom, rushes, sedges, gorse or furzes ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect practical suppression/removal techniques for a long list of pasture nuisances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 3 (best ways of draining marshes, bogs, fens)
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. What are the best ways of draining marshes, bogs, fens, &c. ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document drainage engineering, ditching, and reclamation methods used locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 4 (kinds of grass and which are best)
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. What are the several kinds of grass, and which are accounted the best ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventory grass species and locally preferred varieties for pasture and hay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 5 (circumstances in cutting grass and making/preserving hay)
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. What are the chief circumstances observable in the cutting of grass ; and what in the making and preserving of hay ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record optimal cutting time, methods of curing, stacking, and protecting hay for winter use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enquiries for Meadows — 6 (grass best for winter feeding and for different animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. What kind of grass is fittest to be preserved for winter feeding ? And what grass is best for sheep, for cows, oxen, horses, goats, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather recommendations for species selection for fodder by animal class and for winter preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications and measured performance of M. Villette's burning concave glass
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass is round, rather above thirty inches in diameter; circular steel frame to keep its measure; focus distant from centre about three feet and about the size of half a louis d'or; can burn/melt many bodies; green wood takes fire instantly; one may pass hand through focus if done nimbly but danger in a second; measured times to melt/pierce various materials (examples: small pot-iron melted ~40s, 15-pence silver pierced 24s, thick nail melted 30s, watch spring steel melted 9s, mortar vitrified 52s, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides concrete performance benchmarks (diameter, focus distance/size) and empirical timings for melting/vitrifying various materials; notes practical limitations (focus small so only small pieces exposed) and portability considerations (weighs >100 weight; easily positioned).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for grinding optic glasses of arbitrary conic sections (Hevelius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented a peculiar way of grinding optic glasses; by it it is easy, without considerable danger of failing, to make and polish optic glasses of any conic section, and, what is of most consequence, in any dish of any section of a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reproducible method to produce and polish lenses of precise conic figures (including spherical dishes) reliably; intended for examination by the Royal Society and for practical instrument-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in telescopes using parabolic/figured glasses (Huygens/du Son/de Sons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to grind glasses of a parabolical figure to bring telescopes to perfection; hope to enable discovery with shorter tubes (about one foot) furnished with glasses thus figured than with much longer tubes; report of de Sons producing parabolic oculars and object-glasses with proper figure, polished to admiration, and object-glasses left open without causing any colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for telescope improvement: true parabolic figure, ability to produce short-tube instruments with equivalent/better resolving power, polished finish, control of chromatic/other aberrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for producing lifelike wax models and bas-relief maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to make more lively representations of nature in wax than extant in painting: extraordinary address in modelling figures, mixing colours and shadows, making eyes like nature. New kind of maps in bas relief or sculpture: e.g., isle of Antibe on an ~8-foot square of boards with sea, ships, cannons, tackle of wood fixed upon surface; rocks and island formed exactly, with inequalities, town, fort, houses, platforms, gardens, trees upright in natural colours; men, beasts and protuberances represented; instructive whether viewed horizontally or sidelong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes modelling skill, colour/shadow mixing, anatomical/landscape realism; maps integrate sculptural relief and painted detail for instructive display; suggests scale, framing, and use-case (instruction/visualization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of producing saltpetre in Mogul dominions (extraction & purification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saltpetre extracted from three sorts of earth (black, yellow, white); make two pits flat at bottom (one larger), fill larger with earth, let water run and tread to a pap consistency for two days to extract salt; pass this water into another pit where it crystallizes into saltpetre; to whiten/purify boil once or twice scumming continually and pour hot into earthen pots (~25–30 lb), expose to clear nights so impurities fall, then break pots and dry salt in the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise industrial procedure: selection of earth, leaching by water and treading, crystallization in secondary pit, optional boiling/scumming for purity, pot-crystallization and sun-drying; notes quality differences (black earth best).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational questions to characterise comets (Hevelius' Prodromus inquiries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquires what kind of line comets describe by their motion (circular, straight, curved, partly straight/partly curved); if curved whether regular or irregular, and if regular whether elliptic, parabolical, or hyperbolical; whether comets are in the sky itself (uses parallaxes argument), deduction from a single observation of horizontal parallax and distance (example: deduced distance 5000 semidiameters), estimation of true diameter from distance, whether matter of comets is in the æther itself, whether planets emit exhalations and have atmospheres, whether trains are beams of sun refracted/reflected through the comet's head, whether same comets return, and whether they can be foretold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A methodological checklist for comet study: observational geometry (parallax), path classification (conic sections), physical interpretation (composition, relation to planets and sun), and questions about periodicity and predictability; recommends detailed observations and measurements to resolve these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for evaluating parabolic eye- and object-glasses (de Sons)
rubrics_metrics.description: De Sons produced eye-glasses about 1.5 inches deep and 1.25 inches broad, wrought with a rare steel instrument and polished to admiration; intends to make oculars >2 inches and object-glasses of 5 inches diameter; has begun object-glasses for the ocular ones of the same figure ~2 inches diameter, left open yet without causing any colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation focuses on true parabolic figure, ability to work such cavity without introducing colour (chromatic) aberration, finish/polish quality, and feasibility of scaling to larger diameters.
